newsitem.title: USA: McVeigh's attorney seek delay over victims' ruling.
newsitem.headline: McVeigh's attorney seek delay over victims' ruling.

text.p: Attorneys for Oklahoma bombing suspect Timothy McVeigh on Wednesday asked a federal appeals court to delay Monday's start of his trial until they can challenge a law that allows victims to both view the trial and testify too.
The defence petition was the second attempt in as many days to delay the start of the trial.

McVeigh's attorneys said their client deserves a chance to mount a constitutional challenge to the Victim Rights Clarification Act (VRCA), which specifically allows the victims to view the proceedings and still be able to testify at the penalty phase of the trial if there is a a conviction.

On Tuesday, U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch, taking into consideration the law signed only last week by President Bill Clinton, reversed an earlier ruling and said the victims would be allowed to view the proceedings and testify at the penalty phase.
But McVeigh's lawyers said Matsch's reversal was "misguided."

"Should the VRCA be later declared unconstitutional, the time, energy and resources committed to Mr. McVeigh's trial will have been wasted," his attorneys wrote in a petition filed with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit.

The law Clinton signed barred federal judges from excluding victims who may testify about the impact of a crime on them or their families. The April 19, 1995 bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City killed 168 people and injured hundreds others.

Until the new law took effect federal court rules barred potential witnesses from attending court proceedings before they testified in order to prevent their testimony from being influenced by what they heard. Matsch extended that rule last year, saying victims who attended the trial could not even testify in the penalty phase of the trial, assuming a conviction.
Matsch said a debate on the constitutionality of the new law would delay the trial, a reasoning McVeigh's lawyers characterised as "myopic insistence upon expeditiousness."

On Tuesday Matsch said he could protect McVeigh's right to a fair trial by questioning the victims outside the presence of the jury before they testified to determine if they were unduly influenced by what they heard or saw. But McVeigh's lawyers called this a "Band-Aid."
On Tuesday, McVeigh's lawyers asked the federal appeals court to delay the trial until the court decides if prosecutors must provide the defence with classified intelligence data.
The defence team told the appeals court that it needed the material to investigate its theory that a foreign government, possibly Iraq, may have planned the bombing of the federal building.
